episodes.168496: A complex of storms that moved along the Minnesota/Iowa border surged northeast and began to train across south central Minnesota. Initially, large hail occurred south of Mankato, and around Owatonna. After the initial hail, training of the storms allowed for very heavy rainfall to occur between Waseca and Owatonna. Locally, 2.80 inches of rain fell around Waseca in less than three hours, and a few roads in the city of Owatonna were covered in water.
episodes.168540: Daytime heating, and enhanced low level convergence on differential heating boundaries along two converging rivers, led to an isolated late afternoon severe thunderstorm over lower Richland Co SC.
episodes.168554: A short wave trough produced a band of showers and thunderstorms, with locally torrential rainfall, that moved quickly through during the pre-dawn hours.
episodes.168584: Ahead of a frontal boundary, a line of thunderstorms crossed through the Ohio Valley during the late afternoon of June 13th, moving into northeast Kentucky during the evening hours. Hot temperatures during the day aided with providing plenty of afternoon heating for these storms to continue to develop and persist as the system crossed through the region. Damaging winds were the main concern with this line of storms as it persisted across the Ohio Valley, however frequent lightning also accompanied the storms.||A second line of storms formed along the lingering frontal boundary and pushed through the region during the night of the 13th. Damaging winds were again the main threat with this secondary line of storms. Following this line, yet another round of storms with damaging winds moved through during the early morning of June 14th as enough instability continued to be present across the area. A fourth line then passed through by the later morning hours of the 14th. ||The main impacts from these storms were the numerous trees that were blown down across the region.
episodes.168626: A volatile environment of over 4000 J/KG of SBCAPE, combined with 45 to 60 knots of effective shear set the stage for multiple rounds of thunderstorm during the afternoon and evening hours of June 13th. Initial storms remained poorly organized, but did produce sporadic wind damage or hail. More substantial thunderstorm development evolved during the evening hours in northwestern Indiana and southwestern Lower Michigan and progressed east, eventually producing several swaths of wind damage. The most intense cluster of storms evolved in Berrien county Michigan and dropped rapidly southeast impacting locations extending from South Bend to Fort Wayne. Southwestern portions of Fort Wayne suffered the greatest impacts with widespread tree and structure damage from 80 to nearly 100 mph winds.
episodes.168640: With an area of high pressure still present over New Mexico on June 12, 2022, conditions at the surface still remained too dry for beneficial precipitation. Nontheless, mid-level moisture allowed for the development of high-based, dry thunderstorm activity across portions of central and eastern New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours. This dry activity was prone to producing more gusty and erratic downburst winds, and several stations across Quay and De Baca counties measured wind gusts in excess of 60 mph.
episodes.168641: While mid-level moisture was still present across northern and central New Mexico on June 13, 2022, conditions at the surface and low-levels remained very dry. This led to another afternoon of high-based, dry thunderstorm activity where gusty and erratic downburst winds were the primary hazard. Several stations across the area measured brief wind gusts in excess of 60 mph from these dry thunderstorms.
episodes.168658: Hot and extremely humid surface conditions provided very high instability, while a slowly- advancing warm frontal zone promoted ample vertical wind shear, which led to widespread afternoon thunderstorms along and north of the I-74 corridor.  Storms produced isolated flash flooding as well as marginally-severe winds and hail, over both north-central and east-central portions of central Indiana.
episodes.168695: A supercell thunderstorm moved across northeast Illinois including Chicago and the western suburbs during the late afternoon and early evening of June 13th.  Widespread significant wind damage occurred in many areas and two tornadoes occurred.  Thousands of trees were damaged and hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted.  Several houses were damaged, some significantly, by falling trees.  Numerous vehicles were damaged or crushed by falling trees or tree limbs.
episodes.168764: Ahead of a frontal boundary, a line of thunderstorms crossed through the Ohio Valley during the late afternoon of June 13th, moving into southeast Ohio during the evening hours. Hot temperatures during the day aided with providing plenty of afternoon heating for these storms to continue to develop and persist as the system crossed through the region. Damaging winds were the main concern with this line of storms as it persisted across the Ohio Valley, however frequent lightning also accompanied the storms.||A second line of storms formed along the lingering frontal boundary and pushed into the northern portion of the region during the night of the 13th. Damaging winds were again the main threat with this secondary line of storms. Following this line, yet another round of storms with damaging winds entered along the northwestern portions of the area during the early morning of June 14th as enough instability continued to be present across the area. A fourth line then passed through by the later morning hours of the 14th. ||The main impacts from these storms were the numerous trees and power lines that were blown down across the region. Multiple power outages occurred across southeast Ohio. In Athens County, trees blew down and damaged a deck railing. Following the multiple rounds of storms, a few high water issues occurred in Meigs County.
episodes.168799: Storms that developed in eastern Wyoming continued to move east into the Nebraska Panhandle with hail and strong outflow winds being reported. This included ping-pong ball size hail north of Scottsbluff and over 80 mph winds from thunderstorm outflow near Alliance.
episodes.168828: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm took a similar track to a storm the previous day and caused considerable damage along its track from southern Butte County to southern Meade County, northeastern Pennington County, and Haakon County. The Belle Fourche and Philip areas saw the most significant damage again. Hail near softball size and wind gusts over 80 mph damaged property, trees, crops, and caused widespread power outages.
episodes.168831: A trailing supercell thunderstorm tracked across northeastern Wyoming and across the northern Black Hills and west central South Dakota. This storm brought large hail to the Spearfish, Lead, Deadwood, and Sturgis areas, as well as portions of the southern Meade County plains into south central South Dakota. Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding across portions of northeastern Pennington and Haakon Counties.
episodes.168833: A second severe thunderstorm developed just south of a long-lived supercell over far southeastern Meade County and tracked southeast across far eastern Pennington County and into northern Jackson County before eventually merging with the other storm. This storm produced hail to baseball size along with wind gusts over 60 mph.
episodes.168834: A line of thunderstorms became severe across northwestern South Dakota during the late evening hours. The storms produced wind gusts to 80 mph and small hail.
episodes.168933: Scattered thunderstorms produced sporadic wind damage over portions of the western DC suburbs and near Charlottesville.
episodes.168934: Scattered thunderstorms produced sporadic wind damage over portions of the western DC suburbs and near Charlottesville.
episodes.168975: A convective complex moved east along and north of the Ohio River during the late afternoon and early evening hours.
episodes.168976: A convective complex moved east along the Ohio River during the late afternoon and early evening hours.
episodes.168977: A convective complex moved east along and north of the Ohio River during the late afternoon and early evening hours. Widespread straight line wind damage occurred with numerous wind gusts estimated to be in the 70 to 80 mph range. Over 150,000 customers were without power across southwest Ohio after the storms moved through the region.
episodes.169459: A severe thunderstorm tracked southeast across Lake Michigan, bringing strong winds.
episodes.169754: Rainfall estimates of 2 to 3 inches from thunderstorms during the day on the 13th caused flash flooding on the south end of Porcupine Mountains State Park.  The South Boundary Road was closed from Summit Peak to the Gogebic County line due to water over the road.
episodes.169771: A supercell thunderstorm formed north of a warm front and tracked east across much of southern WI. A swath of destructive hail and sporadic wind damage occurred. More specifically, vehicle, shingle, siding, gutter, and window screen damage. Short segments of tree damage also occurred. Three people drowned in Milwaukee when two men attempted to help a 10 year old boy who had fallen into the rapidly rising waters of a drainage ditch.
episodes.169924: An area of low pressure and associated cold front initiated a vigorous complex of severe thunderstorms across western South Dakota during the evening of June 12th, and these storms tracked east-southeast to affect south central SD after sunset and into the early morning of the 13th. These storms produced destructive straight-line winds of, based on damage assessments, up to 115-130 mph in Jones County, as well as three tornadoes, two of which were rated EF-2 in Jones County following the destruction of property on multiple farmsteads. Additional thunderstorms then redeveloped and reached or nearly reached severe limits across portions of central South Dakota, and training storms brought heavy rainfall of locally 3 inches or more in and around the Pierre and Mobridge areas. Finally, intense non-thunderstorm winds developed on the backside of this system during the early morning hours of the 13th, and impacted much of central and northeastern South Dakota. Some of the peak measures wind gusts include 78 mph five miles SSW of Miranda, 75 mph three miles south of Conde (the roof of a bar was blown off in Conde), and 73 mph six miles SSW of Peever. A Presidential Disaster Declaration was requested and then granted for six counties across South Dakota, Jones and Spink among them, to help residents recover from storm damage that took place from June 11-14th. Initial estimated statewide damage to public infrastructure is assessed at 1.6 million dollars.
episodes.170050: An isolated severe storm moved southeast across Lake Michigan from near Milwaukee and produced numerous reports of large hail up to an inch in diameter and significant wind damage in the form of hundreds of downed trees, tree limbs and numerous power lines from near South Haven southeast to Vicksburg.  Damage was significant and cleanup was still occurring for nearly two weeks after the storms struck.
episodes.170230: Multiple strong to severe thunderstorms developed over Niobrara County in east-central Wyoming with up to tennis ball sized hail on the evening of the 13th.
episodes.170338: Around midnight on this late Sunday night/very early Monday morning, a small complex of severe thunderstorms charged northeastward out of Kansas into far southeast portions of South Central Nebraska, prompting a few reports of severe winds in Nuckolls County. Wind gusts estimated near 65 MPH were reported in and around Superior, and a gust of 58 MPH was measured by a mesonet station located near Nelson.||Upper level flow across the region was southwesterly on the late evening of the 12th, with broad ridging extending north roughly along the Missouri River, while a stronger trough was working inland through the Pacific Northwest. At the surface, low pressure was in place over eastern Colorado, with an eastward extending warm front across central portions of Kansas during the afternoon-early evening hours. With time through the evening, this front drifted into northern Kansas, remaining there through the overnight hours. A shortwave disturbance embedded in the southwesterly upper level flow drove the development of late afternoon thunderstorms over southwestern Kansas, moving northeast through the evening hours. Sustained by healthy warm air advection and convergence along the nose of a 40-50kt low-level jet, this complex of storms entered far South Central Nebraska around midnight CDT.  This activity had no shortage of instability, with most-unstable CAPE values exceeding 4000 J/kg, but deep layer shear was lacking, with 0-6km values around 25-30 knots.
episodes.170339: Mainly between 10:30 p.m and 12:30 a.m. CDT on this late Sunday night/very early Monday morning, a small complex of severe thunderstorms charged northeastward out of southwest Kansas and across portions of this North Central Kansas area, resulting in reports of hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts to around 70 MPH. The brunt of severe weather occurred in Smith County, with the town of Lebanon suffering some structural and tree damage due to estimated wind gusts near 70 MPH. Hail ranging in size from quarters to golf balls was also reported in eastern portions of the county, south of Bellaire and in Lebanon. Estimated wind gusts near 60 MPH were also reported in Jewell County near Esbon and in Mankato.||Upper level flow across the region was southwesterly on the late evening of the 12th, with broad ridging extending north roughly along the Missouri River, while a stronger trough was working inland through the Pacific Northwest. At the surface, low pressure was in place over eastern Colorado, with an eastward extending warm front across central portions of Kansas during the afternoon-early evening hours. With time through the evening, this front drifted into northern Kansas, remaining there through the overnight hours. A shortwave disturbance embedded in the southwesterly upper level flow drove the development of late afternoon thunderstorms over southwestern Kansas, moving northeast through the evening hours. Sustained by healthy warm air advection and convergence along the nose of a 40-50kt low-level jet, this complex of storms first entered North Central Kansas into Rooks County around 10:30 p.m. CDT. This activity had no shortage of instability, with most-unstable CAPE values exceeding 4000 J/kg, but deep layer shear was lacking, with 0-6km values around 25-30 knots.
episodes.170386: A pair of MCVs resulted in severe storms in Iowa on the morning of June 13th. The first moved in from Nebraska and interacted with highly unstable airmass with MLCAPE analyzed at over 3000 J/kg in an area of strong warm air advection. This allowed storms to strengthen and produce nickel sized hail in the early morning. At the same time an MCV was moving into Minnesota with trailing convection into northern Iowa. By mid morning this had also collided with the unstable air with several reports of hail between nickel to golf ball sized in northern Iowa.
episodes.170508: Heavy rain brought flooding to parts of central and southern Arkansas in mid June.
episodes.170579: Thunderstorms developed over eastern Montana into western North Dakota as a surface trough moved through the area. Although some large hail fell with these storms, strong wind gusts became the main impact. The strongest winds were estimated at 90 mph in and around the city of Martin in Sheridan County, where multiple large trees were uprooted, with one tree falling on a structure and damaging it. The largest reported hail also occurred in Sheridan County, which was two inches in diameter. In addition to the hail and strong winds, heavy rain fell on southeast Wells County, with the Johnson Township area south of Sykeston suffering flash flooding with almost all roads having water over portions of them.
episodes.170593: Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over the northern Nebraska Panhandle and tracked east across far northern Nebraska. Wind gusts up to 60 MPH were reported over Sheridan county as well as quarter sized hail in Frontier county.
episodes.170610: A complex of showers and storms moved across southeast Minnesota during the morning and afternoon of June 13th. Rainfall from this activity was generally in the 1.5 to 3 inch range and was enough to cause some street flooding to occur in Winona (Winona County) and send water over some rural intersections southwest of Ridgeway (Winona County) and near New Hartford (Winona County).
episodes.170612: A complex of storms moved across portions of western Wisconsin during the morning and afternoon of June 13th. Runoff from these storms caused some street flooding to occur in La Crosse (La Crosse County). A small shed fire was caused by a lightning strike near Sparta (Monroe County).
episodes.170692: A couple clusters of severe storms moved east and northeastward out of south central South Dakota, evolving into short bowing segments with damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170697: An isolated stronger storm within a line of thunderstorms pushing northeast across northwest Iowa produced sub-severe size hail.
episodes.170699: A low-level jet gradually weakened early morning, but sustained a back-building cluster of thunderstorms across southwest Minnesota within an environment of 1500 J/kg MUCAPE and 40 knots of effective shear.
episodes.170840: On the weekend of June 11th and 12th, a stationary front set up across northwestern Wyoming. On June 12th into June 13th an atmospheric river fed moisture into a powerful jet steam along the front and brought an extended period of moderate rain along with occasional heavy rain due to embedded thunderstorms. ||Preceding this event, April and May were cool and wet, with above normal precipitation and below normal temperatures. This time period included a large storm that brought 2 to 3 feet of snow for many locations above 8000 feet in the mountains of Yellowstone National Park and the Absaroka Mountains. This late season snow event added a large amount of water content to the snowpack.||In the days preceding the flood, many areas experienced well above normal temperatures that brought rapid snowmelt and rises in river levels. In the highest elevations, the snowpack did not decrease notably from the warm temperatures, but was ripened, and primed for later melting due to rain. The rain on the 12th and 13th accelerated the melt and quickly brought rivers over their banks. The result was record flooding, especially across the northern half of Yellowstone. Over 10,000 visitors had to be evacuated from the Park. Numerous roads and trails, mainly in the northern portion of the Park, were damaged or completely washed out. The northern entrance to the Park, which follows the Gardner River through a steep canyon, was completely destroyed in several locations where the fast flowing river's momentum cut into the adjacent steep terrain on which the road was built. The northeastern entrance was also closed due to mud and rockslides as well as flood damage. North of Yellowstone, in southern Montana, rainfall was equally extreme, with communities such as Red Lodge, MT and Gardiner, MT being affected. Flooding and damage also occurred in the southern half of Yellowstone National Park, although damage was much less severe since rainfall was less intense further south.||The extensive flooding and damage led to the entire park being closed for 10 days at the height of tourist season. The southern loop reopened to limited numbers of tourists on June 22nd, and over 90 percent of Park roads reopened by July 2nd. The north and northeast entrances remain closed to most traffic as of early August 2022. A Yellowstone Park press release described the flood as a 500-year flood event. No deaths or injuries were reported from the flooding in Yellowstone. Damages were extensive, but no monetary estimates were available at the time of publishing this report.
episodes.170849: Isolated thunderstorms developed along the Blue Ridge escarpment during the late afternoon and evening and drifted southeast. One of the storms produced hail and brief damaging wind gusts in Oconee County.
episodes.171037: On the evening of the 12th very warm temperatures contributed to adequate instability which help to spark thunderstorm activity across the Texas Panhandle. Although these showers and thunderstorms were not very strong or rain productive, the environment at the surface was very dry. These dry conditions at the surface, provided an environment conducive to strong downbursts winds through evaporative processes. This led to several strong to severe wind gusts across portions of the Texas Panhandle.
episodes.171038: Hot temperatures and drought conditions led to numerous dust devils across the region early in the the summer of 2022.  Clear skies, dry conditions and 100 degree heat provided a day conducive to dust devils in the area.  While not spotted, observational pressure data and remote sensing suggested that a brief rouge wind gust at the Texline West Texas Mesonet was very likely produced by a dust devil.
episodes.171072: On June 12th, showers and thunderstorms developed along a dry line in northwestern Kansas during the evening hours. Thunderstorms in the area produced pea sized hail and wind gusts up to 63 mph. A microburst also occurred in the region that produced damaging wind gusts up to an estimated 80 mph.
episodes.171088: Heavy rainfall culminated with 1 to 2 inches of rainfall in a small basin near Canton on June 12-13.  Brief minor flooding resulted from the rainfall.
episodes.171133: Upper level troughing brought seasonably wet weather with thunderstorms to interior Northern California. A debris flow due to heavy rain was observed in the Dixie Fire burn scar on Hwy 70 in the northern Sierra as well as a record daily rainfall report of 0.47 inches that was set at the Red Bluff Airport.
episodes.171453: A weak cold front pushed through the Western Maine Mountains by late afternoon on June 13th, with a line of showers and thunderstorms sinking south and east.  The storms became stronger once they reached the Kennebec River Valley where a line formed and one of the storms briefly became severe.  The line weakened once again as it approached the coast where the marine layer held strong.
episodes.171542: A volatile environment of over 4000 J/KG of SBCAPE, combined with 45 to 60 knots of effective shear set the stage for multiple rounds of thunderstorm during the afternoon and evening hours of June 13th. Initial storms remained poorly organized, but did produce sporadic wind damage or hail. More substantial thunderstorm development evolved during the evening hours in northwestern Indiana and southwestern Lower Michigan and progressed southeast, eventually producing several swaths of wind damage. In far southern Lower Michigan, damage occurred in portions of Berrien, St Joseph and Branch counties with the most intense occurring from Three Rivers to Sturgis.
episodes.171567: Another trough system brought a round of slow moving stratiform slow moving showers. With the abundant amount of precipitation from earlier in the month, the streams and creeks were already near bank full. The additional 1 inch of precipitation starting to create problems for low lying areas in the Southeast WA and Lower ID Panhandle.
episodes.171568: Another trough system brought a round of slow moving stratiform slow moving showers. With the abundant amount of precipitation from earlier in the month, the streams and creeks were already near bank full. The additional 1 inch of precipitation starting to create problems for low lying areas in the Southeast WA and Lower ID Panhandle.
episodes.171605: A warm frontal moved into the area overnight June 12 into early in the morning on june 13th allowing for thunderstorms to develop. These thunderstorms trained over southern Fairfield County in Connecticut and produced rainfall rates of 1-2 inches an hour. Total rainfall accumulations of 1.5 to 2 inches were reported.
episodes.171619: Multiple rounds of severe storms occurred on June 12, first along a stalled boundary across south-central Virginia in the late morning and early afternoon and then through the afternoon. Enhanced northwesterly flow aloft in the late afternoon and evening allowed for a few supercells as well.
episodes.171692: Ample DCAPE up to 1000 J/kg lead to a number of wind gusts 50-70 mph near the Hwy 83 corridor associated with the aforementioned low level jet south of the surface boundary.
episodes.171705: A few isolated to scattered thunderstorms produced sporadic microbursts with severe wind observations.
episodes.171779: An overlap of high instability and a seasonally strong belt of mid-level northwesterly flow resulted in isolated storms, including a supercell, forming in extreme southeast Virginia and tracking into northeast North Carolina on June 13.
episodes.171780: Isolated storms, including a supercell, formed in extreme southeast Virginia and tracked into the Currituck Sound on June 13, producing gusty winds and a waterspout.
episodes.171826: One to 2 inches of rain fell in Fremont County over a 48 hour period and caused extensive flooding.   A lot of flooding in the Rea area in the Yale Creek estates and Shotgun Complex areas north of Kilgore Yale Road.  Flooding reported at Island Park Village Golf Course. episodes.171832: A persistent upper trough pushed several shortwave troughs supported by a moderate plume of moisture in the middle of June.  Persistent rain showers that develop as a result of each shortwave trough produced enough rainfall for area rivers to swell, with minor flooding being observed along portions of Mill Creek.

The Plumas County Sheriff reported that there were two rock/mud slides and/or debris flows on Hwy 70 one mile west of Belden and near Rogers Flat in the Dixie Fire Burn Scar, with vehicles trapped between the slides. The occupants were rescued, however their vehicles remained temporarily stranded in the area with the road closed for several days. Two flooding issues noted in Winchester. For one property, a gravel driveway was washout due to a plugged culvert. On a neighboring property, a small pond rose six feet and over the roadway. Time of start of flooding was approximate 7pm.

A member of the public in Fort Sumner measured a 64 mph wind gust associated with a dry microburst. One inch diameter tree branches were downed with no other damage reported. Damages are estimated for the tree.
The Columbia Scientific Balloon Facility measured a 66 mph wind gust associated with a dry microburst. No damage was reported.
Mesonet station recorded a 59 mph thunderstorm wind gust at location.

Report received via social media from a trained spotter of a measured 63 mph thunderstorm wind gust at location. Near zero visibility also reported due to blowing dust. Event time is estimated by radar.

An ASOS station near Tucumcari measured a 61 mph wind gust associated with strong downburst winds from nearby shower activity.
A semi tractor trailer was blown over on Interstate 90.
A grain bin was leveled by the winds.

A brief tornado touchdown ripped five large grain bins from their base. The bins were well anchored, in fact, large pieces of cement remained attached to the pins when they were pulled out. The bins were projectiled into two machine sheds and eventually carried about a half mile to the east southeast. Other debris, including a water tank and a dumpster were also tossed east. Other farm equipment was also damaged, including a tipped trailer and displaced grain auger. Pressure change inside the machine sheds also resulted in several combine windshields to be popped out. The house and machine sheds on the property sustained very little wind damage but were built well above normal standards, rated to withstand wind speeds at thresholds of 135 mph and 120 mph respectively.
A semi tractor trailer was blown over on Interstate 90.

The track started near 239th street, about 0.75 miles east of 264th Ave. The path was clearly noted through a shelter belt. The tornado continued another half mile where it damaged a farm. The primary residence had a quarter of the roof panels ripped off a gable style roof and multiple windows and glass doors blown out. Two outbuildings were completely destroyed. Another shed lost the entire tin roof. The debris track from the farm continued for about a quarter of a mile northeast. The resident���s pickup truck also noted damage including the back window broken and dents from flying debris. The tornado weakened, but continued roughly 3.5 miles northeast to Van Metre Rd where it damaged another farm.  At this property a farmhouse had shingle damage to only half of the roof. A well-built machine shed was missing about a quarter of the roof panels. A grain cart was also flipped to the north.

Significant damage occurred along Van Metre road between 234th St and 237th St. This included 3 farms which sustained significant damage. The first farm lost an entire section of roof off an open gable style roof on the primary residence, hay bales were toppled over, a trailer rotated and tipped to the east, a bulk feed bin, along with other debris, was tossed and spread over a half mile east. The next farm also lost panels off the cross gable style roof, dented grain bins, a bent flag pole, a combine header moved 100 yards to the east, and other farm equipment displaced. A deck was completely destroyed. Debris from the farm was spread at least a quarter mile east. The third farm had a feeder wagon flipped, a machine shed completely destroyed, a second outbuilding destroyed and two empty grain bins ripped from the foundation. Debris from the property was spread at least a quarter mile to the east. The damage across these three farms was extensive and was caused by intense and persistent straight line winds. Eyewitness accounts and radar data suggest severe winds stronger than 60 mph lasted for 15 minutes straight with no reprieve. At the peak, winds are estimated to range from 115 to 130 mph. This is concurrent with major loss of roof panels on both homes; both of which exhibited strong roof construction.

The other two men were found June 16th in the same river.

The tornado initially touched down south of the Latham area along Dry Bone Road, State Route 124, and Grassy Fork Road. A path of enhanced tree damage from west of Dry Bone Road to east of Grassy Fork Road was indicative of a weak tornado. This corridor of damage was embedded within a much larger field of wind damage that affected large swaths of Pike County in general.||The more concentrated corridor of damage had a convergent nature to the felled trees, rather defined lateral bounds, and episodes of debris thrown upwind. Most notably, a garage that was heavily damaged on Grassy Fork Road had some of its debris thrown upwind of the storm motion. Several corridors of extensive tree damage between Grassy Fork Road and State Route 124 had a clear convergent pattern in the felled trees. Damage in these areas was consistent with wind speeds of around 90 mph. The tornado likely lifted in the hills east of Grassy Fork Road but the line of storms and significant storm outflow continued to produce widespread straight line wind damage in excess of 70 mph across much of Pike County, including some localized areas possibly approaching 80 mph.

A tornado with peak winds of 80 mph touched down just west of Roselle Road and just south of Lunt Avenue.  Trees were uprooted near Roselle Road just after the tornado touched down.  The tornado caused roof damage to a fast food restaurant building along Roselle Road, just south of Nerge Road.  Sporadic tree damage continued along the path until the tornado crossed Devon Avenue and into DuPage County.
Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Roselle in Cook County.
Wind gusts were estimated to 60 mph.

A tornado with peak winds of 80 mph which touched down in Cook County, crossed Devon Avenue into DuPage County.  The tornado produced only sporadic tree damage in DuPage County as it moved southeast.  The tornado lifted between Sunnyside Road and Turner Avenue, just west of Lake Park East High School.
Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Roselle in DuPage County.  Many roads were blocked by fallen trees.  One tree fell onto a house causing structural damage.
A few trees were blown down and a few power lines were blown down in Prospect Heights.
Video shared on social media showed roofing material blown off an industrial building from north to south near Louis Avenue and Lively Boulevard.
Numerous trees were downed in the Portsmouth area.
Quarter size hail was reported at Route 53 and Lake Cook Road.
The public reported trees snapped in the area.

Scattered tree limbs were blown down in Des Plaines, along with a few large trees.  One tree was blown down in the 700 block of Algonquin Road and another tree was blown down in the 2500 block of Scott Street.

Trained spotters reported numerous trees and tree limbs and power lines down across mainly southern Van Buren county.  Hail up to one inch in diameter was also reported. Two miles west of Lawrence there was a higher concentration of several dozen large healthy tree trunks snapped, uprooted, or large limbs snapped. Damage occurred to at least 3 residences due to fallen trees, one probably a total loss, another with significant roof damage. Cleanup was still ongoing 12 days after the storms struck. Just east of Hartford, hundreds of trees were scattered within approximately a 6 square-mile area with large limbs snapped, trunks snapped, or uprooted. Damage was centered in and near the Van Buren County Youth Fair. The Van Buren Historical Society Museum had damage to the back of the building due to fallen tree limbs.
Multiple trees and utility poles were blown down in Bensenville.
Numerous tree limbs were blown down in Park Ridge.  Wind gusts were estimated to 70 mph.
Trees were uprooted and snapped in Franklin Park.
A photo shared on social media showed large tree limbs blown down west of Elmhurst University.
Several tree limbs were blown down just northwest of Montrose Harbor.
Multiple trees were downed around the city of Greenup.
Multiple trees were blown down in the city of South Shore.
Minor street flooding was reported at numerous locations in Chicago, with most of the reports across north and northeast Chicago.  A few underpasses were also flooded.
Trees were damaged and power lines were blown down in Northlake.

Multiple large trees were damaged across Stone Park, including several large tree limbs one foot in diameter that were blown down.  Multiple cars were damaged by the falling tree limbs.  Damage to shingles occurred to one residence.
Roof tiles were blown off and a window was broken at Value City Furniture in Northlake.
A few trees were downed in the South Webster area.

Multiple trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Berkeley.  Large tree limbs blocked streets near Hawthorn and Morris Avenues.  At least one house had gutter damage from falling tree limbs.
Scattered tree limbs and power lines were blown down between Foster Avenue and Irving Park Road in the Jefferson Park and Portage Park neighborhoods of Chicago.
Tree limbs were blown down and some shingles were blown off roofs in Albany Park.  One tree was uprooted and fell onto a three story building.
Multiple trees were downed near the city of Worthington.
Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down across Bellwood.

A large section of the roof of an apartment building was peeled off, exposing numerous apartments at the corner of 24th Avenue and Washington Boulevard.  Two people in the apartment building were injured.  Wind gusts were estimated between 90 and 95 mph.

Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down across Westchester.  Some trees were uprooted or snapped.  Some trees fell onto houses and onto vehicles.  Many roads were blocked by fallen trees.  Windows were blown out on the second floor of a vacant office building along Roosevelt Road, causing significant wind damage inside the second floor.  Two apartment buildings along Westchester Boulevard had part of their roofs peeled back with debris blown down to the street.  A three foot diameter soft wood tree nearby was uprooted.  A garage was destroyed near Dickens Street and Newcastle Avenue after a large tree fell on it.  Several houses suffered the loss of roof covering in the area of Mannheim Road and Waterford Drive.  Wind speeds were estimated to 90 mph.

Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Broadview.  Photos showed utility poles snapped and blocking a street near 21st Avenue and Cermak Road.  Numerous utility poles were also snapped at 25th Avenue and Cermak Road.
Trees, tree limbs, power lines and light poles were blown down in a swath between North Avenue and Madison Street in the North Austin, Austin and South Austin neighborhoods of Chicago.

Large trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in North Riverside.  The worst damage on the east side appeared to be concentrated between 23rd Street and Traube Street, particularly in the 2300 and 2400 blocks of Burr Oak Avenue and 2500 block of Hainsworth Avenue, where fallen trees blocked roadways.
Photos shared on social media showed multiple trees, tree limbs and power lines blown down, north of 31st Street between La Grange Road and Maple Avenue.
A large tree was uprooted and numerous large tree limbs were blown down in Berwyn.

Extensive tree damage occurred on the west side of North Riverside, from west of 8th Avenue, southeast through the forest preserves near the Caledonia Senior Living Center.  No damaged occurred to the center, but trees were damaged on its grounds and along its edges including damaged fences and access to the facility was blocked.  Numerous trees were fully or partially blown down in the area near Komarek School.
Several tree limbs were blown down south of Fullerton Avenue near Lake Shore Drive.
A trained spotter reported several small tree limbs down as well as a car rolled on its side for an unknown reason.

A large tree from a residential backyard fell onto the wall of the Ames School gymnasium but did little to no damage.  The tree fell onto part of the wall with no windows.  The tree also fell onto a chain-link fence, which was damaged and fell onto a power line.

Hundreds of trees were damaged in Riverside, including trees blown down, snapped and uprooted.  Many roads were blocked by fallen trees.  Eight houses were damaged by falling trees, including homes in the 200 and 300 blocks of East Quincy Street.  A large tree was uprooted and fell onto a house on Lawton Road, severely damaging the home.  Utility poles and powerlines were also blown down.  Numerous roads were blocked by fallen trees and tree limbs.  Numerous trees were blown down onto the railroad tracks near the Riverside station.

A 64 year old man was seriously injured when a large tree limb crashed through his windshield near 31st Street and McCormick Avenue.  The man was a resident of North Riverside and suffered multiple injuries including rib fractures, a fractured arm and wrist, a punctured lung and other internal injuries.

Brookfield Zoo sustained extensive tree damage throughout the park.  Dozens of large trees were blown down and snapped, along with many large tree limbs blown down.  No animals or people were injured and no buildings were damaged.

Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Brookfield.  Some trees were snapped or uprooted.  One tree fell onto a house at the corner of Washington Avenue and McCormick Avenue, damaging the roof.  Some roads were blocked by the fallen trees.  Numerous trees were blown down onto the railroad tracks near the Congress Park station.  A handful of trees were blown down in Kiwanis Park, including an oak tree that snapped 15 feet from its base and landed on the concession stand next to Overholt Field.

Trees, tree limbs, power lines and light poles were blown down in a swath between Division Street and Chicago Avenue in the Humboldt Park neighborhood of Chicago.  At least one large tree fell onto a car, damaging the back end of the car and blocking a road.
Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Lyons.  A photo showed a large tree that was uprooted and fell onto a house.  Two large trees were uprooted, which damaged a sidewalk.

Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Stickney.  Some trees fell onto cars, including a tree that fell on a car in the 3800 block of Wenonah Avenue.  Both front and back windows were shattered and the car was dented.  Structural damage was reported to a hobby shop on Ogden Avenue.  A tree fell onto a house near 40th Street and Euclid Avenue and a large tree was uprooted at 39th Street and Elmwood Avenue.
Trees, tree limbs, power lines and light poles were blown down in a swath between Roosevelt Road and 31st Street in the Lawndale, North Lawndale and Little Village neighborhoods of Chicago.
Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in the north and northeast portions of La Grange.
Multiple trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down in Forest View.
